*Wave 2 design reference — the two modes, the plan artefact and the DAG format.* ➜ **Folded 2026-08-28 into [component-6-engine.md](../architecture/components/component-6-engine.md) §1 and §4**, on T-265, when T-262–T-265 landed and the behaviour the block described became behaviour the code has. The two-mode table, what model-chosen mode does and does not cost, the labelling requirement and the plan artefact's properties are §1; the definition format, its five load rules and `workflow_runner` are §4. The block was folded from *here* rather than from the board because it travelled into the history with T-260's record when the ticket-grain move rule came in on 2026-08-28.

**The last paragraph folded 2026-08-28 on T-266**, when the classifier landed and its four outcomes stopped describing unbuilt behaviour — it is now in [component-6 §1](../architecture/components/component-6-engine.md) beside the two-mode table. The block is fully folded; nothing of it remains here.

*Wave 2 — orchestration (T-260–T-268).* Starts from a no-behaviour-change slice. **T-260 built 2026-07-30** (migration 0035; db 46/46, orchestration 18/18, evals 15/15, full check green).
- **T-260 — The plan artefact, persisted for the existing chain.** ✅ Built 2026-07-30. ⭐ `plans` / `plan_steps` in drawer 3 (drawn first, migration 0035); every run writes a plan whose steps correspond 1:1 to its Step rows. Versioned by supersession, immutable from `ready`. **Acceptance is that the eval smoke set is byte-identical** — this ticket changes no behaviour and must prove it. **Proved:** the smoke result file before and after is identical once uuids and the generation timestamp are canonicalised (a fresh fixture instance necessarily has new ids), and the projection is now pinned as an eval test. Deviations: the 1:1 is against the run's **top-level** Step rows — the delegate step hangs beneath the retrieve step (`parent_step_id`), and a sub-agent's child run carries no plan of its own, because a delegation is not a request. `mode` is `declared` (the coded chain is pre-declared and repeatable) with `workflow_id` null until T-265; `lens_id` null until T-281; `restatement` null until the classifier at T-266 — each recorded as absent rather than invented. **Also fixed a shared-database race the eval harness exposed:** `ingestVersions` walks every version in the database and replaces its chunks wholesale, so a fixture sharing `fake-embed` could be re-chunked underneath a running case; eval fixtures now write their own pinned index (`eval-embed`, ADR-0024). | *(Deps: T-255)*
- **T-261 — Plan read API and permissions.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration. `GET /runs/:runId/plan` → `{ plan, canRerun }`, producer-private on **exactly** the run's own scope: the same `resourceScope`, the same `runVisibleTo`, the same 404 another organisation already gets on `GET /runs/:runId`. Adding no new scope was the point — the plan IS the run's internals, and the 2026-07-12 ruling already decided who reads those. **`canRerun` is on the response rather than derived by the caller**, because reading and re-running are different rights on one record and leaving surfaces to compare participant ids is how one of them eventually offers a button that files a run under the wrong requester; a re-run is a new Run with a new requester, so a colleague reads the plan and gets `canRerun: false`. `canRerunPlan` sits in `plan-writer.ts` beside the writer, so "who may read" and "who may re-run" cannot drift apart in two files. **A run with no plan is a 404, not a null body** — that is a sub-agent's child run, which executes inside a step of its parent's plan, and a delegation is not a request; asserted against a real delegate step rather than a synthesised one. **The eval harness's three recorded absences were closed or narrowed, and the difference matters:** `plan` and `mode` are now read off the record (so `unlabelled` means exactly one thing — no plan was readable — instead of two), `lens` moved from *the case's declaration* to *the run's own recorded lens*, which is the difference between "the case asked for this Lens" and "this Lens produced this answer"; and `workersCalled` **stays null with its reason narrowed to T-269 alone**, because every plan step's `worker` is null until the registry and `[]` would let `expect_not_called` pass on no evidence. T-260's smoke pin was re-expressed rather than loosened: the 1:1 between plan steps and the run's top-level Step rows is now asserted as data in the pinned case. | *(Deps: T-260)*
- **T-262 — Execute from the plan.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration. The chain's ordering left `chain.ts` and became `depends_on` edges the executor walks — four `await`s replaced by a topological walk over `plan.steps`, ties broken on `ordinal`. **The tiebreak is the repeatability guarantee, not tidiness:** two steps with no edge between them are genuinely unordered, and resolving that by row order would make a *declared* workflow non-repeatable, which is the one property declared mode exists to promise. **The ground-check did not move, and that is the ticket.** It runs as code, immediately after drafting, on every answer in both modes; there is no value of `plan.steps` that turns it off, and the plan's `verify` step is the check's **record** — bound to the Step row the check wrote — never an instruction the executor consults. Asserted against a plan declaring `search_corpus → analyse → present` and no `verify` at all: the check still runs, and its Step row comes back **unbound**, which is the honest record of something that ran outside the plan. Without that test the guarantee would have been tested only against the one plan that happens to include the thing, which is not a test. **Refusals rather than repairs, throughout:** a cycle or an edge naming a step outside the plan fails the run before anything executes (half-executing an unorderable plan produces an answer built from an analysis nobody wrote); a `present` step with no drafted claims behind it, and a stage with no executor, both fail loudly with the stage named — the second cannot fire today and fires the moment T-265 or T-266 writes a stage ahead of the code that runs it, which is exactly when a silent skip would be most expensive. **Deviation, stated because it is one ticket early:** `ChainInput.stages` was added now rather than at T-265. Every caller passes nothing and the behaviour is unchanged; it exists because the ground-check guarantee is not assertable against a plan the caller cannot vary. **Parallelism is expressed and not exercised** — the walk returns a linear order and the loop runs one step at a time; ADR-0028 §4's parallel-capable model and the stored `depends_on` both already admit siblings, so the change when they run concurrently is to the loop, not to the ordering or to the record. `openPlan` now returns the step rows it wrote rather than having the executor read its own instructions back out of the store. | *(Deps: T-260)*
- **T-263 — Step and run state migration.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28 (**migration 0055**, drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md) first; generated by `drizzle-kit generate` against the re-synced snapshot and read before applying — it emitted eight `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` lines and nothing else, which is what the T-344 re-sync bought). `step_type` gains the **seven worker types**; `run_state` gains **`completed_with_failures`**. **This is the only migration the whole worker wave needs** — a worker invocation is a Step in the existing append-only tree and, where it delegates, a child Run, which `parent_run_id`/`parent_step_id`/`child_run_id` already carry and the retrieval leaf already does; model, usage, cost, egress, source set and rail outcomes are already columns. **All seven land at once, including the three whose workers are beyond V1** (`authority_lookup`, `web_research`, `verifier`): an append-only audit store cannot be restructured later, so fixing the vocabulary once is ADR-0028 §3's reasoning for the recursive shape applied to the type, and cheaper than widening an enum on a live audit table once per worker. **The anti-drift test is the ticket's other half, and it needed a shape change to be possible at all:** `StepType` was a bare union, which cannot be compared to anything at run time, so "the contracts type and the DB enum cannot drift" was a sentence rather than a check. It is now `STEP_TYPES` (and `RUN_STATES`) as `as const` arrays with the unions derived, and the test compares **all three copies** — contracts, drizzle's `pgEnum`, and `pg_enum` in the live database — because two agreeing proves nothing about the third and the failure mode is a `22P02` at the moment a worker first writes a row. It also asserts `completed_with_failures` is *writable*, not merely declared: an enum value the migration created but the column could not take would pass a set comparison and fail at the first partial run. The worker types are asserted **by name, not by count** — a count passes when one worker type is swapped for another. The test lives in `orchestration` because contracts and db each depend on nothing by the matrix, so neither can check the other from inside itself. `Run.state` is now `RunState`; no semantics change here — which dependants skip and which branches continue is T-268. | *(Deps: T-262)*
- **T-264 — Workflow DAG format, loader and validator.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration. `packages/workflows` was an empty stub and is now the Lens layer's twin — a directory of YAML domain content plus a loader and a validator — deliberately, because two layers a domain specialist edits should not need two mental models. **A workflow definition is a PLAN TEMPLATE:** the plan artefact's step shape with `parameters` where a plan has bound values, which is what makes declared mode evaluable end to end. The type sits in `contracts` for the Lens's reason: three layers need it (`workflows` loads it, `orchestration` turns one into a plan, the API names it on a run) and none may depend on the others. **Each of the five load rules has a fixture that fails it**, because it is easy to write a validator that accepts everything and passes a suite made only of good definitions. **Two rules carry more than their wording.** *Rule 3* is enforced twice over: the type has no `scope` field, so a scope cannot be expressed — and the validator rejects `scope`, `corpus`, `visibility`, `project_id`, `as_organisation` and their relatives **by name**, telling the author *there is no correct spelling of this field*, because the generic "unknown field" message reads as an invitation to find one. *Rule 4* needed a decision the board's block named but did not spell: a workflow declaring `writes: sandbox_document` must declare `label_propagation: refuse | require_override`, which is what it does when its sources' computed label is broader than the destination's (F2) — `require_override` meaning a `label_overrides` row with an author and a reason, never a config key — and **`writes: none` is forbidden from declaring one**, because behaviour declared for a write that never happens goes stale unnoticed. **One rule was added that the block did not name, and it is the sharpest:** a `{{steps.x.output}}` may only read a step the reader **depends on**. The reference resolves to a real step and to one that may not have run — a race dressed as a template, which works in testing and fails the first time siblings execute concurrently. **The registry is injected** (`KnownWorkers`), because T-269 lands after this ticket; T-269 supplies the real one and no signature changes. `definitions/` ships with its AUTHORING.md and no workflows — the first is T-265's. | *(Deps: T-263)*
- **T-269 — Worker registry, typed contract, entitlement assembly.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration (T-263 already carried the step types). ⭐ The declaration type in `contracts`, the registry and assembly rule in `capabilities`, and one worker — `corpus_retrieval`. **The tool set is assembled, not filtered, and the difference is the ticket.** A filtered set is one agent with workers switched off; an assembled set means every user gets a *materially different agent*, built per request. The observable difference is what the model is told, so the guarantee is written into the TYPE: `WorkerDeclaration` has no `enabled`, no `disabled`, no `availableTo`, `assembleWorkers` returns a set rather than annotating one, and a compile-time test pins the absence — a boolean there would be the filtered version wearing the assembled version's name, and something downstream would eventually render it greyed out with a tooltip naming a capability the viewer cannot have. Asserted directly: the serialised assembled set does not contain the excluded worker's name at all. **The three inputs, in order.** No slice → **no workers at all**, not a reduced set and not the read-only ones: someone who cannot reach the project has no agent on it, which is one answer rather than a shorter list. Then the deployment tier — and the sovereign exclusion **reads the router's existing provider-eligibility policy** (`sovereign` permits `self-hosted` only, ADR-0037 §2) rather than a per-worker switch, so a tier added later cannot acquire a web worker by omission. Then the organisation's authority shelf. **Two decisions worth the reading.** (1) **The registry holds only workers that are BUILT** — declaring the other six would put capabilities into the model's tool set that no code implements, which is worse than their absence because the model would call them. The assembly RULE is therefore pure and separately testable, and the sovereign case is tested against a `web_research`-shaped declaration fixture, because testing a rule about a worker that does not exist through the live registry would be testing nothing. (2) **`corpus_retrieval` is not a new path to the store** — it is `groundedLibrary` reached through the assembly gateway, in `targeted` mode, and the test asserts the request it makes has exactly three keys, so the worker cannot have acquired a scope parameter of its own. `capabilities` takes `Assemble` from `contracts` rather than depending on `knowledge`: it depends on the *signature*, which is where ADR-0029 put the guarantee. **What T-272 adds, deliberately absent rather than stubbed:** the `coverage_note`, classification terms, doc types, `include_superseded`, and the scope-keyed cache — a `coverage_note` saying something plausible and untrue would be worse than the field not existing. The registry satisfies T-264's `KnownWorkers` unchanged, so a declared workflow now validates against the real set. The eval harness's `workersCalled` deferral was narrowed again, from T-269 to **T-265**: the registry existing does not put a worker's name on a plan step — the declared workflow does. | *(Deps: T-248, T-263)*
- **T-265 — `workflow_runner` and the first declared workflow.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration. The coded chain, written down as [project-question.yaml](../../packages/workflows/definitions/project-question.yaml) — same four stages, same order, **changing no behaviour**, which is asserted as a comparison rather than a claim: the same question through an app composed with the workflow registry and one composed without it returns the same answer, the same step rows and the same run state, and differs only in what the *plan* records. What the plan gains is `workflow_id` + `workflow_version` (null since T-260, and the T-260 record predicted exactly this) and a `worker` on the retrieve step. **`workflow_runner` is the one non-leaf worker, and the exception is narrow:** it executes a pre-declared DAG and cannot compose one, which is why it is not the generic escape hatch non-negotiable 8 forbids. The board says keeping it that way is review discipline, not a test — true of the intent, so what the tests hold instead are the two *structural* halves: it takes a workflow id rather than a step list, so there is no shape in which a caller hands it an improvised plan, and `bindWorkflow` adds, removes and reorders nothing. **It refuses an unbound required parameter** rather than substituting one, and the message carries the parameter's own user-facing description — a declared workflow run on a parameter nobody supplied answers a question nobody asked, and reading like a real answer is what makes it expensive. (T-266's outcome 2 is the other half of that refusal.) **Two validator refinements came from declaring a real workflow rather than from review**, which is the case for building one rather than a plausible one: `worker` became **optional** — `analyse` is the orchestrator's own thinking leaf and `present` is citation resolution (ADR-0027 §6), and a worker is a tool the agent may *call*, which is not what drafting is — and a `verify` step may **never** name one, because the ground-check is code outside the plan and that step is its record, so naming an executor for it would suggest something that could be asked not to run. **A deployment without the registry falls back to the coded chain**, identical in every stage, which is what makes "changes no behaviour" true of a deployment mid-rollout too; a declared workflow that *cannot bind* is a 400 naming the parameter and never a quiet fall-through, because falling through would answer under a plan the user did not get. `ASK_WORKFLOW_ID` is config, not code. **The eval harness composes the app the way a deployment does** — the dependency matrix was widened for `capabilities` and `workflows` on exactly the reason that admitted `@infora/api`: a case running the fallback while production runs a declared workflow is evidence about a configuration nobody ships. **`expect_calls` / `expect_not_called` are live at last**, three tickets after T-256 implemented them: `workersCalled` reads off the plan's steps, and **null and `[]` stay different observations** — `[]` from a plan that was read is the honest "it called no worker", null is "no plan was readable", and collapsing them is the vacuous pass the deferral existed to refuse. **The Wave 2 fold-in happened in this commit**, per the register: the two-mode table, what model-chosen mode does and does not cost, the labelling requirement and the plan's four properties into [component-6 §1](../architecture/components/component-6-engine.md); the definition format, its five load rules and `workflow_runner` into §4. **One paragraph deliberately did not fold** — T-266's four classification outcomes — because folding unbuilt behaviour into a component doc makes that doc assert what the code does not do; it stays here with a pointer until the classifier lands. | *(Deps: T-264, T-269)*
- **T-266 — Model-chosen orchestration and mode labelling.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration. **Classification is ADR-0027's *code with an LLM escape hatch*, not the reverse, and that is the ticket's central decision.** Whether a question *matches* a declared workflow is judgement in language and is the model's; whether the workflow's parameters are *bound*, which workers the requester is *entitled* to, and what the plan therefore *is* are definite questions with right answers and are code — a model asked those would be spending money to be less reliable. **The deterministic default is not a stub:** with one declared workflow whose parameter is the question itself, asking a frontier model to choose among one option is exactly what ADR-0027 exists to prevent, so `singleWorkflowClassifier` matches when there is one option and defers only when there is a genuine choice. **The four outcomes are a union, not a boolean plus extras**, because each carries different evidence and a caller that could ignore the difference would eventually label one as another. **What the classifier is allowed to see is the security half:** the worker set handed to it is the one already *assembled* for that requester (T-269), so the model is never told an unentitled worker exists — the assembled-not-filtered rule reaching the one place it would be easiest to lose, a tool list. Asserted at the HTTP boundary, not only in the unit. **A classifier naming a workflow the deployment does not carry falls through rather than failing** — the answer still gets produced, and the weakness shows up in the metric built to catch it rather than as a 500. **The fall-through rate is now a reported metric** (`fallThroughRate`, over *labelled* runs only, null rather than 0 when nothing was labelled). It survived the eval report's no-aggregate guard on a stated distinction: the banned number is a pass rate across categories, which hides a bad category behind a good one, and this measures *which mode ran* rather than how well anything did. It exists because the classifier's failure is quiet — a weak one routes everything to model-chosen, every answer still arrives grounded and cited, and nothing goes red. **The guarantees are identical across modes, and that is asserted rather than asserted-in-prose:** a model-chosen run's ground-check completes with rail outcomes even where the planner declared no `verify` stage at all, which is the strongest form of "a planner could skip it". **Three deviations, each with its reason.** (1) **Outcome 2 has no clarification dialogue** — Wave 6 is deferred beyond V1 — so V1 does what Wave 6 specifies for a user who *skips every question*: proceeds on stated assumptions, named at the top of the answer rather than in a footer, drawn from the parameter's own user-facing description (which is why T-264 requires that description to be copy). (2) **"Mode on Teach submissions" has nothing to attach to** — Teach is Wave 7, deferred beyond V1 — and "on the footer" is T-294, which reads the mode off the plan this ticket writes. (3) **Where an out-of-scope refusal belongs in the run record is unruled**, so nothing is written today (the reversible choice) and it is **`Q-048`**. `ASK_WORKFLOW_ID` survives as an override rather than the default: pinning every Ask turn to one workflow is what the deployment did between T-265 and T-266. **The Wave 2 fold-in completed here** — the four classification outcomes into [component-6 §1](../architecture/components/component-6-engine.md), the half T-265 deliberately left behind because folding unbuilt behaviour into a component doc makes it assert what the code does not do. | *(Deps: T-265)*
- **T-267 — Plan edit and re-run.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration — migration 0035 already made `state` and `superseded_by_plan_id` the only two columns a sealed plan may change, and its CHECK already required each to imply the other, so supersession was drawn before it was needed. `POST /runs/:runId/plan/rerun` takes an edited step list and produces **a new run with a new plan, with the old plan marked `superseded` pointing at it** — the plan that produced the first answer stays exactly as it was, because a plan is evidence and *"what did your AI do"* has to survive the user editing it afterwards. **An edited plan is `model_chosen` even though it started `declared`, and that is not bookkeeping:** a declared workflow's promise is that the same inputs produce the same steps in the same order, and a hand-edited copy makes no such promise whatever it still resembles, so it may not carry the label; `workflow_id` goes null, which the stored CHECK independently requires. **The two bounds are the ticket.** *Entitlement:* the only list a worker name may come from is the set **assembled** for this requester (T-269), and the refusal names what IS available — which is that requester's own set, so nothing about anyone else's entitlement leaks by saying it. *Scope:* a scope field is refused **by name, in every spelling** — `scope`, `projectId`, `corpus`, `as_organisation` and the rest — with the workflow validator's own reason, that there is no correct spelling of it, because the generic unknown-field message reads as an invitation to find one. That is what makes "editing cannot widen scope" structural rather than checked. **The strongest test is the removed `verify` step:** a user editing the ground-check out of their own plan is the sharpest available form of "a planner could skip it", and the check still runs (T-262) with its Step row unbound. A `verify` step naming a worker is refused with the same rule the DAG format holds. **403, not 404, for a colleague** — deliberately, and against the usual principle-4 reflex: this caller can already *read* the plan, so telling them it does not exist would be a lie they can check, and principle 4 exists to hide what someone cannot see rather than to confuse them about what they can. An unexecutable edit (no `present` stage) is a 400 carrying the executor's own reason, so the request fails rather than half a run existing. | *(Deps: T-266)*
- **T-268 — Partial failure semantics.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration (T-263 carried `completed_with_failures`). A failed step no longer stops the run: the step and its plan step are recorded failed, **its transitive dependants are skipped, and independent branches carry on**. The closure has to be transitive — skipping only the immediate dependants leaves a step two edges downstream to fail on an input that never arrived, which reports one outage twice under two different names — and a **join** downstream of a failure is skipped even where its other input survived, because a join that ran on half of what it declared would produce an answer nobody could account for. **Three run states, and the middle one is the ticket:** `failed` where nothing survived (an incomplete answer offered as a complete one is the failure this slice exists to avoid), plain `completed` where nothing failed (the third state is not the new default, asserted), and `completed_with_failures` where an answer exists *and* something did not run — reporting that as `completed` hides it, and as `failed` throws away work the user can act on. **The answer BODY reports what did not run, not only the footer.** This is absence detection applied to the system's own failures: an answer that silently omits what a failed step would have contributed reads as a complete answer and a reader has no way to know otherwise, and a footer will not do, because it is read after the answer has already been believed. The stages are named in words (*"the library search step failed"*), since this text reaches the user. **Two things sharpened rather than added.** A dependant is now `skipped` where it used to be left `pending` — `pending` reads as *"not reached yet"*, which is a claim about a run that has finished. And **a plan with no `present` stage is refused before the walk rather than after it**: that is a defect in the plan, not a failure during it, and spending a retrieval and a model call to discover it would be paying for the discovery (T-262's test was rewritten to assert the sharper behaviour). **The guarantee did not move:** where drafting fails the ground-check does not run, and that is untouched — there is no *answer* to check, and "every answer is ground-checked" says nothing about a run that produced none. **One correctness fix found by the rewrite:** the first cut treated `cited.answer === null` as "nothing survived", which would have failed every document-targeted run, where a null answer beside suggestions is the normal shape. `completed_with_failures` is an **error** for an eval case, stated rather than incidental: a case is evidence about an answer, and an answer produced while part of the plan did not run is evidence about something else. | *(Deps: T-266)*
- **T-270 — SPIKE: locator extraction.** ✅ Findings 2026-08-01 — [spike-locators.md](spikes/spike-locators.md). Research, no code. **Three findings against the running pipeline, each checked rather than reasoned about.** (1) **A chunk is not a substring of its version** — the splitter consumes the whitespace after a terminator and the packer rejoins with a single space, so a blank line between paragraphs becomes `" "` and `indexOf(chunk.content)` returns `-1` on any chunk whose interior crossed a paragraph break. Every after-the-fact offset-recovery scheme is built on that. (2) **Heading numbers are read as sentence terminators** — the split fires after the `2.` of a numbered heading, gluing the heading to the previous paragraph. A retrieval-quality bug that will be blamed on the embedding model, and it destroys the one signal (`§12.4.7`) that is the most useful locator a consenting document has. (3) **A cross-boundary quote is in no chunk *and* in no version** — the join the model saw was reconstructed by the packer and never existed in the source, so the obvious fallback ("if not in a chunk, look in the version") fails on exactly the case it was introduced for. **Per format:** docx gives **paragraph index** for the cost of not throwing it away, gives a section number only where the author *typed* it (`<w:numPr>` is resolved by Word at render time), and gives **page not at all — a docx has no pages**, so any "page 14" from a Word source is an invention. PDF gives exact page numbers and **has no ingest path whatsoever**, existing only as an output rendition. **That last row is the commercially significant one:** a real scheme's 100–500 documents are overwhelmingly PDF, page is the locator a planner actually uses, and *"a 100–500 document corpus"* and *"citations that resolve to a locator inside the source document"* cannot both be true through the docx path alone. **Recommendation for T-271: store a character-offset range on `version_chunks` and derive everything else from it** — exact, format-agnostic, and nearly free, because findings 1 and 3 are both consequences of discarding information the chunker holds at the moment it packs. The board should stop describing the gap as "locators" and start describing it as **"offsets now, pages later"**. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-271 — Locators through the ingest pipeline.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-04** (migration 0039, drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md) first; data 23/23, knowledge 28/28, api 256/256, e2e 55/55, full check green). Locator capture persisted on `version_chunks` and carried to the assembled passage, plus the verbatim fallback. **The quoted passage must be findable in the source document** — a quote that cannot be found is worse than none, because it looks checkable. Built to [spike-locators.md](spikes/spike-locators.md)'s recommendation, which **closes with this ticket**: `start_offset` / `end_offset` on `version_chunks`, everything else derived. **Offsets are captured in the chunker and nowhere else, because nowhere else can:** the splitter eats the whitespace run after a terminator and the packer rejoins with one space, so a chunk whose interior crossed a paragraph break is *not a substring of its own version* and `indexOf` returns `-1` (T-270 finding 1). **The refusal is the ticket's weight, not the happy path** — a locator is emitted only when the stored span is demonstrated to still point at the passage (compared whitespace-insensitively, since that difference is the chunker's own), and otherwise the citation degrades to **version grain** rather than rendering one nobody can follow. Finding 3's cross-boundary quote resolves as the spike predicted: the span runs first-chunk-start to last-chunk-end, a real range even where the model's rendering of the join never existed. `paragraph` is derived; **page and section are absent rather than guessed** — a docx has no pages. `AssembledItem.locator` fired `wall.test.ts`'s pinned key set by design, and it is an output-side field like `chunkId`. **Two spike items are deliberately elsewhere:** the heading-number split is **T-307** (the spike argues for its own commit, because re-chunking moves embeddings and the eval seed set is the instrument), and PDF input is **T-305**. | *(Deps: T-270)*
- **T-276 — SPIKE: the authority corpus.** ✅ **Findings 2026-08-27 → [spikes/spike-authority-corpus.md](spikes/spike-authority-corpus.md).** `authorityRef` runs through contracts, the citation table and the ground-check, but there is no store — the canon half of Ask has no data, and the type admits a citation the product cannot produce. Licensing is ruled (two-tier); the spike names the v1 standard-tier instrument list with a licence basis for each, the in-force interval model, and org-tier ingest. **Four findings, and two of them change what T-277 should build:**
  **(1) The standard tier rests on one licence basis** — Crown copyright under OGL v3.0 covers the Act, the SIs, the NPSs, the Advice Notes, s.51 advice, made DCOs and Decision Letters. **Three carve-outs matter more than the list:** OGL does not cover third-party material *inside* an OGL document (an NPS figure, a reproduced BSI table), which argues for provision-grain licence attribution; **Decision Letters name people**, so T-277 introduces a store of named individuals and must register it in [personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md) *before* loading one; and the list is deliberately England-and-Wales-shaped, which closes ADR-0023's open jurisdiction question with a recommendation rather than a silence.
  **(2) 🔒 "In force" is two time axes, and the useful one cannot be computed.** The *text* interval (when this wording was the wording) is what legislation.gov.uk answers. The *applicability* rule — which cohort of applications an instrument governs — is a transitional provision, and **the instrument in force today is frequently not the one governing the scheme being asked about**. Nearly every real consenting question is of the second kind. So: store the text interval, **carry the transitional note as text beside every hit**, and compute applicability **never** — it depends on facts about the application, and appearing to know it would be the expensive kind of wrong. The unit is a **provision**, not a document: an Act is not in force, its sections are, on different dates and with different extents.
  **(3) The org tier's real problem is what *counts* as authority**, not ingest — the extractors and the loud refusal already exist (T-305/T-306). ADR-0023 §2's test is three facts (an issuing body, a version, an in-force date), and **requiring all three at ingest is the enforcement**: without it, "add to my authority shelf" becomes a way to make a firm's own method document citable, which is the laundering ADR-0026's filters exist to prevent arriving through a door nobody was watching. Plus a **licence-type attestation** — BSI and ISO licences are commonly *single-user* and the org tier makes text reachable by every participant, so the question moves from "nobody asked" to "they said corporate" for the cost of one radio button.
  **(4) 🔒 The corpus must NOT live in `version_chunks`.** That table is under RLS and every read goes through `deliverableVisibleSql`, a predicate built entirely around project material. The standard tier is deliberately outside per-tenant access resolution and the org tier is walled by a *different* rule — so putting authority chunks there means either widening the wall predicate to admit rows it was not written for, or carrying a corpus with no wall inside the table whose whole purpose is enforcing one. Separate tables **from the start**: the cost of separating later is a migration, and the cost of not separating is a wall predicate with an exception in it. Sizing does not argue otherwise — the standard tier is 100–200 documents, smaller than the pilot's own library. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-281 — `packages/lenses`: loader, validator, one Lens wired.** ✅ Built 2026-08-01. ⭐ A leaf package depending on `contracts` only; the definitions and their authoring guide already sat at [`packages/lenses/definitions/`](../../packages/lenses/definitions/) (moved 2026-07-31) and this ticket built the package around them — `package.json`, the matrix entry, the loader and the validator. **A Lens whose prohibitions try to weaken a shared-core rule fails to load**, with a message naming file, field and rule in language a domain expert can act on. **The reach guarantee landed in three independent places, none redundant:** the type-level signature test (`reach.test.ts` — `Assemble` takes one argument and `AssemblyRequest` has no room for a Lens), the dependency matrix (`contracts` only, so the package holds nothing with which to narrow a retrieval), and a **new RULE 3 in `scripts/source-rules.mjs`** — `governance`, `knowledge` and `data` may not mention a Lens at all, which is what covers `resolveAccess` and `groundedLibrary`, whose signatures are not in contracts and so cannot be pinned from a test. **The core-negation check is deliberately narrow, and says so:** it matches the shape a weakening prohibition actually takes — the suppression of a required disclosure — and its real regression guard is `definitions.test.ts`, because a validator that fires on a *good* prohibition lands on a domain expert who did nothing wrong. Writing that test found two genuine false positives in the first draft of the patterns; both are recorded in `core.ts` beside the pattern that replaced them. **Deviations:** (1) `example_exchanges` is counted as **declared, not as successfully parsed** — an author who wrote two and left a `why` off one is told about the `why`, not also told to write two they can see they have written; (2) the loader's `production` flag **defaults to true**, the fail-safe direction — a deployment that forgets it loses hot reload rather than gaining draft Lenses in front of a customer. **One Lens-validation rule is deferred, explicitly:** "`preferred_workers` naming a worker not in the registry fails to load" cannot be enforced, because there is no registry until T-269 and all four active Lenses name `corpus_retrieval`, `authority_lookup`, `extractor`, `verifier`. The field loads as unvalidated strings against a stated deferral naming T-269; every other validation rule — unknown field, missing field, enum, duplicate id, filename/id disagreement, core-negating prohibition, `active` with fewer than two `example_exchanges` — is enforced now. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-299 — The Lens through the request and into the prompt.** ✅ Built 2026-08-01. ⭐ The plumbing between a validated Lens file and an answer that reads differently — **four pieces no other ticket owns**, found in the 2026-07-31 MVP review, all four landed. (1) **Contracts + API:** `lensId` on the create-run body; an unknown id is a **400, refused before the run opens** — never a silent fall-back to a default, because a Lens the user did not get is worse than a refusal. `400` not `404`: the Lens set is not access-controlled, so naming the id leaks nothing and `not_found` would wrongly imply it might exist for someone else. (2) **The chain:** the Lens travels as *data* through `ChainInput` → the draft leaf's input → `groundedDraft`, not as a construction argument — the draft leaf is built once at app composition (`createDraftLeaf`), so a Lens bound there could never be per-request. (3) **The prompt:** `composeSystemPrompt` puts the core first, states the precedence in a sentence rather than leaving it to ordering, then appends the overlay. The core clauses are held as an **array rather than a joined string**, so composition is checkable by containment; the hostile cases are **built in code, bypassing T-281's validator**, because "cannot be authored" and "cannot succeed" are different guarantees and only the second is worth resting a claim on. `@infora/capabilities` was widened to see `@infora/lenses` — safe in one sentence, since `lenses` is itself confined to `contracts` and grants no reach. (4) **The evidence:** `plans.lens_id` / `lens_version` written from the request rather than the hardcoded null. **Acceptance is the pair, and both halves are asserted at the HTTP boundary:** the same question under two Lenses returns two visibly different answers *and* an identical source set, plus the four-Lens form that is `PERM-05`'s API-level twin. **Two deviations.** (a) The API rejects **what the registry does not carry**, rather than checking `status` itself — in production the two are identical (no drafts are in the registry) and outside production the draft is deliberately reachable, which is what AUTHORING.md's "put it in with `status: draft` and open Ask in a test environment" depends on. Implementing the literal wording would have made the authoring guide's own workflow impossible. (b) `fakeRouter` gained a **function form** taking the system prompt, because a router that ignores its prompt can prove neither half of the acceptance. | *(Deps: T-281)*
- **T-282 — The four active Lenses and the draft.** ✅ Built 2026-08-01. Planning & Environmental, Engineer, Project Manager, Communications, plus the deliberately-incomplete Commercial. The files were authored and ready; this ticket made a Lens something a *case* can run under, and turned the worked exchanges into the register guard. **The runner** now resolves `lens:` against the harness's own registry — loaded with production semantics, so a case cannot reach the draft `commercial`, and an unavailable id is an `error` **naming the ids that are available** rather than an opaque `400`. **The report gained §4.1's per-Lens table**, deferred at T-257 for want of anything to key on: a Lens whose register cases regress while another's improve is exactly the result an aggregate would hide, and the Lens layer's whole claim is that the four differ. **`LENS-01`–`LENS-04`** are the guard itself — *the same question, the same corpus, the same acting user, four Lenses* — because one Lens case in isolation proves only that *a* Lens applied. ✅ **The grader choice is ruled and recorded** in [evals/README.md](../../evals/README.md): **human review for the MVP.** It was not really a fork — an independent family needs a second provider (behind the infra gate) *and* a family-aware router (T-284/T-286), so "configure one" was not available to this ticket, and shipping it as a decision would have been shipping one nobody could act on. The four cases therefore return **`ungraded`** and block the gate, by design. **What stays machine-checked meanwhile:** each case carries a plain substring beside its `~claim` asserting the Lens **reached the prompt at all**, because a silently-dropped Lens and an ungradeable one would otherwise produce the same verdict, and they are very different failures. **Deviation, and it belongs to the fixture not the Lenses:** only four of the twelve worked exchanges are expressible against `hollowfield-reservoir`, which is two documents sized for a permission case's access graph. The rest ask about noise chapters, Rochdale envelopes and Deadline 3. That is [v1.md](v1.md)'s own *"a few hundred fixture documents, not five"* obligation, and it is a fixture-sizing ticket rather than anything the Lens layer can fix. **One thing to watch:** the harness's fake chat now prefixes the reader named in the system prompt — but **only when a Lens is present**, so a no-Lens run returns the original reply byte for byte and T-260's smoke-result pin stays valid. | *(Deps: T-299)*
- **T-283 — Lens switching, persistence, logging.** ✅ Built 2026-08-01. **The MVP's last Wave-4 ticket.** Switching re-renders the next answer only; history keeps the Lens that produced it. Default is config, not code — `DEFAULT_LENS_ID`, reported by the new **`GET /lenses`**, which is deliberately *not* project-scoped and *not* access-resolved: the Lens set is a property of the deployment and identical for every requester, because a list that differed by who asked would make a Lens a reach control. It carries **summaries only** — prohibitions and worked exchanges are prompt material and do not leave the server. Persistence is **per run, in the plan record** T-299 writes — no new column and no conversation-level Lens. The picker rides [ask.tsx](../../apps/web/src/screens/ask.tsx) as a chip; the full composer treatment is T-292 and is post-MVP. **Three decisions worth reading.** (1) A misconfigured `DEFAULT_LENS_ID` reports **null**, not the typo — preselecting an id the run endpoint would then refuse is a worse failure than preselecting nothing. (2) The Lens is captured **at send time**, so switching mid-flight cannot relabel an answer already being produced. (3) A **reopened** conversation shows no Lens per answer rather than guessing: the Lens lives on the plan and the plan read API is T-261, so `null` means *not known*, and inventing the picker's current value would be a fabrication about a past answer. **The e2e earned its place immediately:** `/lenses` was missing from the vite proxy allowlist, which does not error — it returns `index.html`, which parses as "no Lenses" and renders **no chip at all**. A silent, plausible-looking nothing that no unit test could see, because they call the API directly. **Also fixed, and unrelated:** `smoke.spec.ts` asserted the seeded consultant has one Participant, stale since T-298 gave her a second scheme for the conflict register. | *(Deps: T-282)*

*Wave 5 design reference — task-class routing, folded 2026-07-31.* **Route on task class, not on perceived difficulty; the routing table is configuration, not code.** Two axes in a fixed, non-negotiable order: `tier policy filter (hard, fails closed) → task-class selection → dispatch`. The first axis is already built — the router enforces deployment security tier before any task-based optimisation (ADR-0037 §3) and fails closed rather than falling back to a non-conforming region or provider to preserve availability. **This wave adds the second axis only:** `Router.chat(task, request)` already accepts a task argument and currently ignores it — the seam exists, the routing does not.

| Task class | Tier | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `orchestrate` — classification, intent, workflow selection | frontier | judgment-heavy, user-visible, decides everything downstream — not the place to economise |
| `clarify` — question generation and recommendation | frontier | the recommendation is doing the teaching; a weak one damages trust more than a slow one |
| `plan` — step selection in model-chosen mode | frontier | same reasoning |
| `triage` — retrieval relevance filtering | small, fine-tuned where available | highest volume by far. **This is where gross margin lives** |
| `extract` — schema extraction | mid, structured output | high volume, low judgment, verifiable against the schema |
| `synthesise` / `synthesise_long` | frontier (large context for long) | user-visible prose under a Lens |
| `draft` — grounded document drafting | frontier | the existing chain's one thinking leaf |
| `verify` — claim verification | frontier, **different family from the producer** | independence; same-family verification is largely self-agreement |

*Configuration shape:* `defaults {fallback_attempts, timeout_ms}` then one entry per task class — `primary {family, model}`, `fallback[]`, `max_tokens`, and for `verify` the `constraint: different_family_from: draft`. **Hot-reloadable in non-production, immutable for the process lifetime in production** — the same rule as Lens and workflow definitions. **Fine-tuned models are pluggable but optional: the system must run entirely on frontier models with a config change**, so the absence of a fine-tune is never a blocker — with the corollary that every eval case runs against the *configured* table and records which, because a pass on a fine-tuned triage model is not evidence about the frontier-only configuration.

*Wave 5 — model routing (T-284–T-286).*

### Raised during the build

- **T-298 — Seed the conflict-register scenario; deterministic participant order.** ✅ Built 2026-07-30. A second client and scheme, so an exclusion has two projects to pair; `readMe` ordered by `created_at` because twelve e2e specs index `participants[0]`. **Fixed a T-247 regression:** under RLS a DELETE must first *find* its rows through the SELECT policy, so ingest's replace-wholesale step deleted nothing and re-insert collided — ingest had become silently non-idempotent. The existing test would have caught it, but turbo had **cached** `@infora/data`'s result from before the migration; turbo keys on file hashes and cannot see database state. | *(Deps: T-245, T-247)*

*Where the design documents went (2026-07-31):* the Ask specification is **folded into this board and deleted**. Its design content lives in the wave reference blocks and the ticket entries above; the Lens definitions and their authoring guide moved verbatim to [packages/lenses/definitions/](../../packages/lenses/definitions/); the eval harness's machinery is documented beside the code it describes at [evals/README.md](../../evals/README.md). Decisions stay in the ADRs and vocabulary in CONTEXT.md, as they always did — those were never the specification's to hold. As each area is *built*, its reference block condenses into the built ticket's own entry, the same way T-255–T-258 already have.

### Waypoint A — the pilot floor

- **T-300 — The three-organisation seed.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-04** (no migration; e2e 55/55 with a new `three-organisations.spec.ts`, full check green). **Org C is Redgate Ecology**, a new organisation rather than a promotion of **Halvern Associates** — Halvern's documented meaning is *"an organisation with no Membership at all"* (T-022's wall subject), and reusing it would delete a test subject in order to create one. Seeded with its own org admin (Nadia Okonjo), Participant (elevated, as Org B's lead author is), a single-org sandbox with a working document, and **`WA-ECO-PEA-001`, produced and shared with nobody** — the missing `deliverable_shares` row *is* the negative. **The spec asserts the positives too:** Trentmoor sees the deliverable because it owns the library (producer | project owner | live share, ADR-0016 as data), so the test cannot pass against a broken project — only the share is absent. Org B's half of the negative is created **at runtime rather than seeded**, so it is live work rather than a fixture. `SEEDED.thirdOrg` was left alone and commented: it means Halvern, *outside* the project, and the new persona is `SEEDED.secondConsultant`. The dev seed carries an owner and two members on one project so the wall is **demonstrable in the customer's own tenant** — a screen the buyer can look at, not a property they take on trust. Mirrors the Session B design story exactly (Org A owner, Org B consultant, Org C brought in to probe cross-organisation sharing), and **B↔C invisibility is the thing a consultancy will actually poke at**. Seed the third organisation with its own user, Participant, sandbox and at least one deliverable it produced and did **not** share, so the negative is demonstrable rather than merely absent. **Two of the three are operator-held or fictional** ([v1.md](v1.md)) — this is a demonstration, not a commercial proof, and the entry must say so where an operator will read it. **Do not extend the e2e specs that index `participants[0]`** without re-reading T-298: the order is deterministic by `created_at` and a dozen specs depend on it. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-301 — The elevated tier: close-as-rejected and owner supersede/withdraw.** ✅ **Ruled 2026-07-31** (recorded against the tracker's existing 2026-07-18 QA-themes entry): the destructive actions are gated on **`Participant.elevated`**, audited, with **org admin deliberately not extended** — being able to manage an organisation's people is not the same authority as being able to end a deliverable. Surface the affordance as **absent rather than disabled** for an unelevated Participant — the same principle as an unentitled worker (T-269) and a non-conforming model route (T-292). ⚠ **Re-cut 2026-08-04 — the ticket's premise was stale and two thirds of it is already built.** It says *"what does not exist is any path that checks it"*; **T-174 and T-176 built those paths.** `close-rejected` checks `slice.elevated` ([cycle.ts:1076](../../apps/api/src/cycle.ts#L1076)) and withdraw/restore check `canEditPlan` ([plan.ts:343](../../apps/api/src/plan.ts#L343)), and both surfaces already hide rather than disable ([cycle.tsx:177](../../apps/web/src/screens/cycle.tsx#L177), [plan.tsx:516](../../apps/web/src/screens/plan.tsx#L516)). **What is genuinely outstanding is two things, and they part company:** (a) **the refusal audit** — ✅ **built 2026-08-04**, migration 0038, drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md) Drawer 2 first. `elevated_refusals` is append-only on the T-008 trigger, because a refusal record a super-user could quietly delete is worth nothing and the people who hold this tier are exactly the people who would want to. Participant grain, not User — the tier is a *project* capability. `required_tier` is stored although one value is possible today, so a row still means what it meant once a second tier exists. **`container_restore` is recorded although it is recovery rather than destruction** — the record answers *"who attempted an act this tier holds and was refused"*, and one direction of the same gate going unrecorded leaves it incomplete while looking complete; plan-metadata editing rides the same predicate and is deliberately out. **A cross-organisation attempt is not recorded** — it is answered `404` above the tier check, and logging it would record an act against a container the requester was never shown. (b) **Supersede, which does not exist at all** — nothing in the codebase sets `containers.state = 'superseded'`, and building it means creating **the first cross-organisation container write**, which is 🌫 **fog until `Q-036` is ruled**, per the Q/T boundary rule. `supersede` is deliberately absent from the `elevated_action` enum for the same reason: a value the schema carries and no code can set is a claim the schema makes falsely. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-302 — Incremental ingest: a version id, not a full-table walk.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-03.** 🔒 **The single highest-leverage fix in this slice, and it is small.** `ingestVersions` walked **every version in the database** on each call, chunking and embedding in a serial in-process loop, and ran on library admission. At the skeleton's few dozen rows that is invisible; at 500 documents the per-admission path is roughly **125,000 version re-ingests**, and even one call at the end leaves every subsequent admission re-ingesting all 500. **This was not theoretical:** on 2026-08-01 the shared dev database reached ~1,050 versions and the api suite began failing on 5-second timeouts in the cycle tests — always the ones that admit a version to grounding. **Two entry points, not one** ([contracts.md](contracts.md)): `ingestVersion(db, router, versionId)` on every product path, and the sweep surviving as `ingestAllVersions` under a name that says what it does — reachable from the ingest CLI and the e2e substrate, which index a seeded database from nothing, and from nothing on a request path. An unknown id **throws** rather than indexing nothing quietly. **A version is indexed when it comes into existence, not when it starts grounding** — ingest excludes nothing, exclusion being retrieval's job (ADR-0022, T-033) — so all three version-creating acts ingest: the sandbox freeze, promotion, and the contractual revision an accepting verdict issues. **That closed a real gap the sweep was masking, and it is the reason this ticket is three call sites rather than one:** a promotion onto a container already in the library makes a new version current, and its chunks previously arrived only at the *next* acceptance anywhere in the project — between the two, the deliverable's current version had no chunks and it **silently dropped out of retrieval**. `cycle.test.ts` now pins that case. Each call sits after its transaction commits; an outbound embedding call holds no transaction open. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-303 — The bulk-load path.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (no migration; api 374/374, full check green). A corpus load is an **operator action, not an interactive one**, and must not run through the per-admission path at all.
  **A CLI, not an endpoint** — `pnpm --filter @infora/api run bulk-load -- --project … --organisation … --directory …`. Nothing that is allowed to take hours belongs on a request path, and there should be no endpoint until someone can say what the surface does while it runs. Each document is one `ingestVersion` (T-302), so a 500-document load is 500 targeted ingests and steady state is one.
  **Resumability is the part that is easy to get wrong by doing less.** The obvious check — *"does a container with this reference exist"* — is wrong, and wrong in the direction that hides the failure: a document whose container committed and whose embedding call then died is **in the library, listed, and answering nothing**, which is worse than absent because the list says it is there. So the resume check is *"is this document's current version indexed under the pinned model"*, and a re-run reports three distinct outcomes — `present`, `reindexed` (it finished a half-landed document), `loaded`. **`isVersionIndexed` lives in `@infora/data`**, not here: `scripts/source-rules.mjs` RULE 1 caught the first draft reading `version_chunks` from `apps/api`, correctly. It scopes its read, because the index is under RLS and the policy **fails closed** — an unscoped read answers "never indexed" for everything and re-embeds the whole corpus on every resume.
  **What it admits is T-304's ruling, built:** a library-scope container, `in_library`, `live`, one genesis version `R01` — and **no work item**, which is the entire distinguishing fact. No new state, no new table, no marker column. `producing_organisation_id` is *whose material this is*, so the wall reads received material on the existing predicate with **no carve-out** — a carve-out here would be a hole in the one predicate grounding, the library list and citation resolution all share.
  **The reference is the file name, and that is a decision.** The project's naming scheme composes codes for *planned deliverables*; generating a scheme-conforming code for a consultee response would dress received material up as a deliverable, which is the laundering T-304 exists to prevent. The file name is also what makes the load resumable at all — it is the only identifier stable across re-runs.
  **Refusals are per document and named twice:** in the line as it happens, and again in a closing block that says plainly *"these documents are NOT in the corpus"*, because a 500-line log with forty refusals scattered through it is a log nobody reads to the top of. **A non-zero exit** is the difference between "the corpus is loaded" and "the corpus is loaded except for the forty nobody was told about". A duplicate reference *within one run* is refused rather than silently resolved — it is a different fault from a re-run and deserves a different answer. | *(Deps: T-302)*

  *What the ticket asked for, kept as the standard it was built to:* admit N documents as reference-material containers (the 2026-07-31 ruling) in one pass, ingesting each **once**; [operating-envelope.md](../architecture/operating-envelope.md) measures this separately from interactive ingest and **allows it hours**; what it may not do is block an accepting action or leave the corpus half-indexed on failure — a partial load must be resumable and must say what it did not load.
- **T-304 — Reference-material containers, and the marker that keeps them distinguishable.** 🔒 ✅ **Ruled 2026-07-31 (Claude's call, owner-delegated):** a legacy corpus is *received* material, not *produced* material, and V1 must not invent a lifecycle to admit it. It enters as **reference-material containers** — admitted to the library with a single genesis Version at `live`, so it grounds (ADR-0011) and rides every existing access and state pre-filter unchanged, but carries **no work item**. The ADR-0032 addendum already establishes that reference-material containers have none and that surfaces must never assume the link, so **the distinguishing fact is an *absence***, exactly as ADR-0038 made `container_id` the sole distinguishing fact for a bound sandbox document. No new state, no new table, no parallel lifecycle. **One consequence is build work, not a note:** a loaded reference document must be **visibly** distinguishable in the Documents view from an accepted deliverable, or the corpus quietly launders itself into the produced record. That marker is part of this ticket, not later polish. | *(Deps: T-303)*
  ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (no migration; api 377/377, e2e 63/63, walkthrough recaptured, full check green).
  **`LibraryItem.kind` is derived and nothing is stored** — the left join to `work_items` answering null *is* the marker, so there is no flag a writer can forget to set and no second definition to drift. The test pins that the two rows differ in the work item **and in nothing else**, `metadata` included.
  **Two tables, not a badge in one.** The ruling's failure mode is laundering, and a badge inside a table headed *Live deliverables* still lists a consultee response as a live deliverable. So reference material has its own section, and its **columns differ because the facts differ**: no Suitability and no Discipline (received material carries neither), no Transmit (this project did not produce it and has no standing to issue it), and *Held by* rather than *Producer* — the organisation named holds the document, it did not write it. The section is absent entirely on a project that has loaded none.
  ⚠ **The seeded library turns out to be reference material, all of it** — the seed's own comment has said so since it was written (*"the seed library is owner-added reference material (ADR-0011)"*), and the Documents view has been listing it under *Live deliverables* the whole time. Nothing changed except that the screen now says what the data always meant. The recaptured walkthrough shows the two genuinely produced deliverables above five received documents, which is the first time that page has been honest about the difference.
  **The premise checked, because it is only sound in one direction.** The ruling reads the absence of a work item as "reference material", which holds only if every *produced* library deliverable has one. In the built flow it does — a plan row creates the container and its work item together, and promotion promotes a planned container — so the marker is sound. Worth stating rather than assuming: nothing *enforces* it, and a future path that admits a deliverable without a plan row would mislabel it. If that path is ever wanted, it needs a constraint, not a second marker.

*The corpus's format reach (T-305–T-307).* [v1.md](v1.md) rules format coverage **narrow — text-extractable only, an unsupported document failing loudly and per-document** — and [spike-locators.md](spikes/spike-locators.md) found what that currently means in practice.
- **T-305 — PDF text extraction on the ingest path.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (migration 0048, drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md) Drawer 2 first; api 372/372, data 15/15, e2e 63/63, full check green). 🔒 **The commercially significant gap T-270 found.** PDF existed in the codebase only as an **output rendition** (`textToPdf`); there was no PDF *input* path at all. A real scheme's 100–500 documents are overwhelmingly PDF — issued deliverables, Advice Notes, Decision Letters, consultee responses — and **page is the locator a planner actually uses**, and the only format that has one (a docx has no pages: pagination is computed by the viewer, so any "page 14" from a Word source is an invention). *"A 100–500 document corpus"* and *"citations that resolve to a locator inside the source document"* cannot both be true through the docx path alone. Text-extractable PDFs only; a scanned one **fails loudly, per document**, per the ruling — OCR stays out of V1.
  **The page locator needed no column, and that is T-271's rule paying off rather than a shortcut.** [`pdfToText`](../../apps/api/src/pdf-text.ts) terminates every page with a **form feed inside the extracted text**, so page is *"count the separators before the span, plus one"* — the same derivation as paragraph, over `chr(12)` instead of `E'\n'`, computed in the same query. *Store the position, compute the view* meant the second locator dimension cost one SQL expression. A version with no form feed anywhere reports **no page**, which is every docx and always will be: absent still means absent.
  **Where extraction sits was the ticket's one real decision.** It is at **upload**, not in the ingest sweep, and the reason is structural rather than preference: `versions` is append-only (T-008) and `versions.content` is both what the chunker indexes and what every locator is an offset *into*, so extraction must precede the version that carries it — the sweep cannot write one. A PDF also has no conversion path to extract it later, deliberately (ADR-0004 — the PDF is the record rendition, never an editing surface), so it is text at upload or never. What T-302 kept off the request path is the corpus-wide walk; this is one bounded document. **The bulk-load path (T-303) calls the same extractor** and inherits the same refusals.
  **The extractor is hand-written, and that is a deliberate divergence from the spike**, which called a PDF extractor *"a real dependency, not a refactor"*. [`upload.ts`](../../apps/api/src/upload.ts)'s zip reader and [`xlsx.ts`](../../apps/api/src/xlsx.ts)'s workbook reader made the same call twice already, and what is needed here is text and page boundaries out of the text-extractable subset — not rendering, not layout — which does not justify taking a rendering engine into a deployable meant to run in a sovereign tier. It sweeps the file for objects rather than following the cross-reference table (real exports arrive with broken ones), expands object streams, decodes Flate and the three ASCII filters, and reads text through `/ToUnicode` CMaps and font encodings. **Glyph advance widths turned out to be load-bearing, not polish:** a browser positions each glyph individually, and without the widths the extracted text reads *"t h e a s s e s s m e n t"* — the pen position alone cannot tell a space from kerning.
  **Every failure is the whole document, by name.** `pdf_no_text` (the ruling's scan), `pdf_encrypted`, `pdf_unreadable`, `pdf_unsupported_filter` — and a content stream that will not decode refuses the **document**, never the page, because a corpus that answers confidently out of the pages it happened to read is exactly the failure the loud-and-per-document rule exists to prevent. The sandbox's multi-file upload was changed to match: it **runs to the end and reports each file by name**, where before the first refusal aborted the batch and named nothing. A refused document is written nowhere — no opaque blob parked in the sandbox for someone to miss. The test suite proves this against a **real browser-printed PDF** committed as a fixture, not only against our own writer's output, because reading back what `textToPdf` wrote proves the reader agrees with the writer and nothing about a client's corpus. | *(Deps: none; wanted by T-271)*
- **T-306 — xlsx and pptx text extraction, and the loud per-document refusal.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (no migration; api 391/391, full check green). Both upload today and neither converts (`unsupported_conversion`), so they sit in the sandbox as opaque blobs and never ground. Extract text — sheet-and-cell for xlsx, slide-and-placeholder for pptx — which also gives each its natural locator. **The refusal path is half the ticket:** [v1.md](v1.md) requires an unsupported document to fail **loudly and per-document**, and a bulk load of 500 that silently indexes 460 is the failure mode — the corpus then answers confidently from a library missing the forty nobody was told about. | *(Deps: T-303)*
  **The natural locator turned out to be the one that already existed.** A sheet and a slide are each a *paginated unit* — the thing a reader names when they say where something is — so both render **one per page** with T-305's form feed between, and the page locator T-271's stored span already derives addresses them unchanged. **Four formats, one locator mechanism, no new field and no migration.** A slide is the cleanest case of all: `page` *is* the slide number, with nothing lost in translation.
  **A row is a row, not a list of cells.** `A1: Reference / B1: Respondent` embeds as coordinates rather than as meaning, and nobody cites a spreadsheet by cell — a planner cites *"the consultation register, the Environment Agency's row"*, which is that row's own text. So the row is the passage and the verbatim is a line a reader recognises. **Cell-grain addressing is not delivered and deliberately not half-delivered:** it needs a locator that is a coordinate rather than a count, which is a different mechanism and should be asked for before it is built.
  **Slide order comes from `presentation.xml`, not from the file names** — a reordered deck still stores its slides in creation order, and slide number *is* the locator, so it is the one thing that must not be guessed. **Speaker notes are not read:** they are the presenter's script, not the document, and indexing them would put words in the corpus that nobody in the room ever saw.
  **Two refusals worth naming.** A workbook of charts and formulas is refused `xlsx_no_text` — and the gate counts **rows, not characters**, because every workbook has tab names and "is there any non-whitespace" passes a chart-only file on the strength of the word *"Chart"*. A deck of images is `pptx_no_text`, the pptx form of the scanned PDF the ruling names.
  ⚠ **One asymmetry, deliberate and stated:** a **docx still keeps `''` at upload** while the other three extract. It is the only uploaded format with a conversion path, and that path makes its text *canonical* rather than merely grounding — extracting at upload too would give `content` two meanings for one format. The bulk load has no such exception and reads every format, docx included, because reference material never converts.
  **Found while consolidating:** the zip reader had been copied into `upload.ts` and `xlsx.ts`, and **the copies had drifted** — the xlsx one inflates with a bounded output length and a try/catch, so a crafted entry cannot balloon kilobytes into gigabytes, and the docx one did not. Both read untrusted uploads. A third copy for decks would have been a third chance to be the unhardened one, so there is now one reader (`zip.ts`) and it is the hardened one. `parseXlsx` also generalised from *the first tab* to *every tab, named* — corpus extraction wants all of them, and two walks of the same relationship graph would be two chances to disagree about which tab is which.
- **T-307 — Chunker: stop reading a heading number as a sentence terminator.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (no migration; data 25/25, full check green; eval seed set run either side — see the caveat below). [spike-locators.md](spikes/spike-locators.md) Finding 2.
  **The spike's proposed fix was narrowed, deliberately.** It asks for *"a digit, then whitespace, then a capitalised word"* — but that also matches every ordinary sentence ending in a number, so *"The predicted level is 54. The barrier is three metres."* would stop splitting: one retrieval bug traded for a commoner one. **What separates a heading from a sentence is not the digit — it is that the number starts its line**, so the test is anchored there: a run of digits and dots, at the head of a line (indentation allowed, prose not), ending in the dot in question. A form feed counts as a line start too, so a chapter opening a PDF page is covered — T-305's page separator earning its keep a second time.
  ⚠ **The instrument was weaker than the spike assumed, and saying so is the point.** The seed set was run before and after and is **unchanged — 6 pass, 0 fail, 0 error**. But **11 of its 17 cases are `ungraded`**: they need a model grader and none is configured, so what was actually compared is the deterministic half — one happy case and the five permission cases. Those five are about *reach*, which re-chunking cannot move, and HAPPY-01 asserts **recall only** (T-312 records why). So this run proves *no regression in access or retrievability*, and it does **not** measure retrieval quality, which is the thing the change was made to improve. The measurement the spike wanted needs **T-312**'s larger fixture and a configured grader; until both land, "run the evals either side" buys less than it sounds like. | *(Deps: none)* `SENTENCE_BREAK` fires after the `2.` of a numbered heading, so a heading is severed from its own section and glued to the tail of the previous paragraph — *"…the NPS. 2. Method"* becomes one chunk. **A retrieval-quality bug that will be blamed on the embedding model**, and it destroys the one signal (`§12.4.7`) that is the most useful locator a consenting document has. The fix is a lookahead. **It changes chunk boundaries, therefore embeddings, therefore what retrieval returns** — so run the eval seed set (T-259) before and after, and do it in its own commit rather than folded into T-271's offsets. Explicitly out of scope: resolving Word's `<w:numPr>` list numbering, which means implementing Word's numbering algebra and is its own ticket if it is ever wanted. | *(Deps: none)*

### Waypoint C — the product surface

- **T-308 — The rulebook's home.** ✅ **Unblocked 2026-08-01 → [ADR-0048](../architecture/adr/0048-the-checker-findings-not-prose.md).** The rulebook is **guiding-channel material in org context, in its entirety** — a house drafting manual is the firm's own preference document, not a published external instrument, so it fails the 2026-07-29 ruling's operative test on its own terms. Build the loader and the org-context binding. **The part that is not obvious:** a finding may quote it **verbatim without citing it**, so the loader must preserve enough structure to quote *a clause* (§4.2, not "page 11") — a rulebook chunked for steer alone would make the ruling unimplementable at the surface. | *(Deps: none)*
  ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (migration 0051, **drawer 7 — Context**, the first store any of component 4's three scoped stores has ever had). Until this landed `guiding` in the assembly gateway returned an empty array *because there was nothing to return*: the ticket reads as one binding and was in fact the whole channel's first data.
  🔒 **The not-obvious part is the design, not a caveat on it.** The stored unit is the **clause**, not the chunk — [rulebook.ts](../../packages/data/src/rulebook.ts) sits beside `chunker.ts` and deliberately is not it. `chunkText` trims sentences and rejoins them with a single space, so a chunk is **not a substring of its own source** (T-270 finding 1) and carries no clause address at all; quoting from one would produce a rule the manual does not literally contain. A test asserts exactly that difference. Splitting is anchored to the **line**, which is T-307's lesson borrowed from the other side: what separates a heading from a sentence is not the digit but that a heading number starts its line — a "digit, dot, capital" rule would carve a rulebook at every measurement in it. A clause with no number is stored with **none rather than a guessed one**: it still steers, it simply cannot be quoted with a reference, and the load reports how many *can* be, so an org admin learns their manual is unquotable at upload rather than from a finding that reads oddly six weeks later.
  **The org-context binding is one key: the organisation.** No project, no share, no acknowledgement, no wall predicate — *portable to every project the organisation touches* (ADR-0020) **is** the query. Asserted both ways: the same firm's people reach it on a second project, and a rival on the **shared** project reaches none of it (ADR-0048 §6 — a competitor's drafting standards are the ethical-wall breach nobody thinks of as crossing the wall). These rows are **not in `version_chunks`**, applying [the authority-corpus spike](spikes/spike-authority-corpus.md)'s Finding 4 a store early.
  ⚙ **One contract change, and it is the ADR made structural.** `AssembledItem.source` is now **optional**, absent meaning *not citable* — `source` is what a citation resolves to, and guiding material never is (ADR-0021, ADR-0048 §5); previously every guiding item was forced to carry a source identity it had no business having. The clause address lives in a new `rule` field instead, pairing with T-328's `RulebookEvidence`, deliberately outside `source` so it cannot resolve like a source chip. `wall.test.ts`'s pinned item shape fired on both, which is the review that pin exists to force.
  ⚠ **`Q-046` raised, and it constrains T-310 rather than this.** The rulebook rides the channel *in its entirety* and is not retrieved against the question, so the token budget is the only thing that narrows it — and `mergeChannels` drops guiding before grounded. For an Ask answer that degrades tone; for a **checker**, whose silence is a claim, *"no findings against your drafting manual"* after reading three-quarters of it is indistinguishable from compliance.
  **Scope calls:** an org-admin door exists (`POST`/`GET`/`DELETE /organisation/rulebooks`, the `/organisation/users` tier, multipart through the same extractor and the same vocabulary of refusal the corpus path uses) but **no UI** — there is no org-administration screen in the product, and inventing one is not this ticket. Retire, never delete: a finding written against a rule the firm has since withdrawn must still resolve to the words it quoted. The original bytes are **not kept** — what steers is the clause text, and a blob nothing reads is a deletion obligation nothing needs.
- **T-328 — The finding schema.** The type both the checker DAG and the findings surface stand on, in `contracts`, minted **ahead of** them because they cannot be specified without it. A finding carries: the **input it arose from** (corpus / attached / rulebook, which decides its citation treatment), an **anchor** at the locator grain T-271 establishes, a **severity**, its **evidence**, and an **optional proposed revision** expressed as a Suggestion rather than as free text — the ADR-0048 constraint that keeps the checker from acquiring its own write path. **Severity's vocabulary is this ticket's call** (ADR-0048 leaves it open deliberately: it is a naming question, not a design fork) — pick the smallest set that a reviewer can triage by, and resist per-organisation configurability until someone asks. | *(Deps: T-271)*
  ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** — [packages/contracts/src/finding.ts](../../packages/contracts/src/finding.ts), types only, no migration and no endpoint.
  **Severity is `required` / `advisory`, and the argument for two is that a third has no work to do.** The reviewer's triage question is single — *must this change before the draft goes out, or may I reasonably decline it?* — and a middle level answers neither and becomes the drawer everything ambiguous is filed in. **Neither word is a verdict**, which is what ruled out `critical / major / minor`: those grade the *document*, and a finding states a defect and never a verdict. And **`required` is deliberately not `blocking`** — ADR-0049 §7 blocks promotion on an **open** finding of any severity, so naming one level "blocking" would imply the other is not, which is the exact confusion §7 exists to prevent. One vocabulary for everyone; per-organisation configurability refused.
  🔒 **ADR-0048 §7 is carried as a TYPE, not as a rule to remember.** `evidence` is a union discriminated by the input the finding arose from, so a rulebook finding has **nowhere to put a `Citation`** — the dishonest object does not compile, and the test file's `@ts-expect-error` lines are the acceptance. That is §5's quotable-but-never-cited ruling made structural rather than documented.
